elements.name: Sodium
description: ) meaning "a kind of saltwort", from which soda was obtained, of uncertain origin.
symbolOrigin: The original source is either the Arabic word

content: is the Latin name of "a compound of sodium".

deeper.text: Soda came through Italian from an Arabic name of salt-tolerant plants (suwaydāʾ, the seablite genus Suaeda). Their ashes gave soda ash, which was also made from saltworts.
Another explanation derives it from Arabic suda, "headache", as soda was a remedy for it.
The symbol comes from natrium, named after natron, the salt the ancient Egyptians mined for burial rites, Egyptian nṯrj. It passed through Greek nitron, so nitrogen has the same root.
Magnesia was named after the Magnetes, an ancient Greek tribe mentioned in the Iliad. Their colonies in Anatolia bore the same name.
The word magnet has the same origin, "stone of Magnesia". The sources differ on whether that means the Greek region or its colony in today's Turkey.
Latin alūmen literally meant something like "bitter (salt)" and is related to the English word ale.

elements.name: Chromium
description: ), "colour", because of its multicoloured compounds. This word was adapted as the French

deeper.text: In antiquity two black minerals from the lands of the Magnetes were both called magnes. The "male" one attracted iron and gave us the word magnet. The "female" one did not, and it was later called magnesia, from which manganese developed.
Old English īsern goes back to Proto-Germanic *īsarną, borrowed from Proto-Celtic *īsarnom, possibly related to a word for "blood". The Wikipedia table gives "holy or strong metal" instead.
Latin ferrum is of unknown source, perhaps a loan from a pre-Latin language. One proposal connects it to Phoenician barzel, "iron".

deeper.text: German Kobold, "goblin": silver miners in the Harz used the word for rock laced with arsenic and sulfur, which spoiled the ore and made them ill.

deeper.text: Not "copper-colored ore", as the Wikipedia table has it. German miners called the ore Kupfernickel, "copper goblin", blaming a mischievous sprite as they could get no copper from it. Cronstedt shortened the name in 1751.

deeper.text: Copper comes from Latin aes Cyprium, "Cyprian metal", after the Greek name of Cyprus, a major source of copper in the Bronze Age. The word Kypriot is attested in Mycenaean Greek of the 15th century BC.

The origin of the name Cyprus itself is unknown. Proposals include an Eteocypriot word for copper, perhaps related to Sumerian zubar (copper) or kubar (bronze), the Greek name of the henna tree, and a Semitic goddess.

deeper.text: Moscow takes its name from the Moskva River. The most widely accepted theory derives it from a Proto-Balto-Slavic root related to "wet", so it might mean a river at a wetland. Wiktionary gives Proto-Slavic *mosky, "swamp, dampness".
A Finno-Ugric hypothesis derives it from Mustajoki, "black river".
